quiz.question: What is the average life expectancy worldwide today?

headline: Humanity Added More Years in One Century Than in the Previous Two Thousand
teaser: If you were asked to guess the average lifespan of a human being on Earth right now -- not in your country, but globally, across every nation, rich and poor -- what number would you reach for? Most people, when confronted with this question, consult a mental model that was last updated somewhere around 1985 and has been quietly gathering dust ever since. The actual figure tends to provoke one of two reactions: either disbelief, or the slightly unsettling realisation that the world has been changing underneath your assumptions without bothering to send a notification. Two-thirds of people guess too low. The question is: how low?
metaDescription: Global average life expectancy has reached 73 years — double what it was in 1900. Two-thirds of people guess too low.
summary: In 1900, the average human could expect to live to about 32. Today, global average life expectancy stands at approximately 73 years. That is not a gentle upward slope — it is the single most dramatic improvement in the basic terms of human existence ever recorded. And most people, when asked, guess the figure is at least a decade lower than it actually is.
nuance: The 1900 figure is heavily influenced by infant mortality; adults who survived childhood lived considerably longer. COVID-19 caused a temporary dip from 73 to 71 in 2020-2021 before recovery began. Regional gaps remain vast — Sierra Leone's life expectancy is 55, Japan's is 85.
aside: Consider that for most of recorded history, a human being's odds of reaching fifty were roughly equivalent to a modern person's odds of being struck by lightning twice. We have changed, in the span of a few generations, the fundamental arithmetic of being alive.

emailDigestLine: Humanity doubled its average lifespan in one century. It took the previous hundred thousand years to get to 32.
premiumTeaser: The story of how we doubled the human lifespan involves, in no particular order: a Viennese doctor who was mocked to death for suggesting that hand-washing might help, a retired military engineer who accidentally revolutionised sewage, and a statistician whose bar charts caused a national scandal. It is, in the proper sense, extraordinary.
b2bClassroomNote: Classroom discussion: Ask students why the 1900 figure seems so low (infant mortality effect). Connects to SDG 3 and introduces the concept of life expectancy as a composite measure. Pair with Gapminder's Trendalyzer for interactive exploration.
publishingNote: UN and OWID data are closely aligned. COVID dip noted in nuance. Strong Bryson-style aside.

learn.title: Hans Rosling's 200 Countries, 200 Years TED Talk
learn.description: Rosling animates two centuries of life expectancy and income data in four minutes flat. It is the single best visual explanation of how the world went from 32 to 73 — and why the change feels invisible.

fund.description: Clean water and sanitation are behind a disproportionate share of this chart's upward slope. WaterAid works in the countries where waterborne disease still drags life expectancy down.

act.action: Write to your water utility asking for their latest water quality report
act.description: Safe water is the foundation of the life expectancy gains on this chart. Knowing what is in your own tap water connects the global story to your postcode — and the reports are public, even if nobody reads them.
